<HistoricalDocument xmlns="http://example.com/historicaldocument">
  <Metadata>
    <Language>Hebrew</Language>
    <WritingDirection>rtl</WritingDirection>
    <PhysicalDescription>Single manuscript leaf, ink on paper. Some ink smudges and minor wear.</PhysicalDescription>
    <Description>Rabbinic ruling (responsum) regarding the procedures for appointing community leaders (Parnasim) in Frankfurt, detailing an agreement and subsequent clarifications. Dated 18 Elul 5421 (corresponding to 1661 CE).</Description>
    <Script>Hebrew</Script>
  </Metadata>
  <Page>
    <Header>
      <FolioNumber>עשו</FolioNumber>
    </Header>
    <Body>
      <MarginalNote placement="left_margin">
        <Line>1661</Line>
      </MarginalNote>
      <Heading type="main">
        <Line>העתק מגוף הפסק שנפסק בעניני הפרנסות מן ה"ה אב"ד ובר"י פה מהר"ר מענדל פס י"ץ בצירוף הב"ד.</Line>
      </Heading>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>נדרשנו לאשר שאלו לנו מחמת מינוי הפרנסים פה ק"ק ורנקבורט ע"י פשר בשנת שפ"ח ע"י הגאון מהר"ר חיים כ"ץ ז"ל שהיה אז אב"ד פה ובצירוף בני ישיבה והפרנסים ועיקורי קהל</Line>
        <Line>והעשירים שהיו בזמן ההוא כמבואר בפנקס הקהל באריכות ואח"כ נתחדשו איזה תיקונים בענין מינוי פרנסים ע"י ט"ו אנשים שנתחברו בשנת תח"י לפ"ק כמבואר ג"כ בפנקס הנ"ל</Line>
        <Line>בכן כהיום הזה מחמת איזה טעמים ונימוקים וטובת קהילתינו יצ"ו עלה על דעת מקצת אנשים לעשות פרנסים באופן זה, דהיינו שמונה פרנסים מן השנים עשר פרנסים יהיו גבאי</Line>
        <Line>קהל להיותם פרנסים החודש ולהתנהג בהנהגתם ככל אשר מוטל על הגבאים לעשות, כגון לעשות סגן וכיוצא בו, והארבעה הנותרים לא יהיו פרנסי החודש, ובשאר דברים</Line>
        <Line>יהיו כשאר הפרנסים שיהיו תמיד במושב הפרנסים ולא יעשו דבר זולת הארבעה הנ"ל. בכן באו בשאלתם לחוות דעתינו אם הדבר הזה הוא נגד החרם שהחרימו</Line>
        <Line>הקדמונים שבפשר הנ"ל, כי אין רצונם לעשות דבר נגד החרם הנ"ל ונגד חרם ט"ו אנשים הנ"ל.</Line>
        <Line>תשובה כפי אשר הורונו מן השמים, כי הן אמת שאין לעבור על החרם שבפשר הנ"ל וכן על חרם ט"ו אנשים כלל. אמנם אופן הנ"ל, דהיינו שיהיו שמונה אנשים פרנסים גבאי'</Line>
        <Line>כנ"ל וארבעה הנותרים לא יהיו גבאים כנ"ל, אינו נגד החרם הנעשה בשנת שפ"ח ואינו נוגע בו כלל ויכולים לעשות מינוי פרנסים באופן זה. אמנם אותה התקנה</Line>
        <Line>שנעשה ע"י ט"ו אנשים כנ"ל, שלא יתבררו שני פרנסים מהפרנסים ישנים שהיו בשלשה שנים שעברו בתוך הפרנסים אשר יבררו בשלשה שנים הבעל"ט כמבואר בפנקס</Line>
        <Line>הקהל, מצאנו שאותן שני אנשים לא יהיו במינוי השמונה פרנסים ולא בתוך מינוי הארבע אנשים, רק יהיו לגמרי חוץ מהחברותא ולא יהיו להם מינוי בתוך החברותא.</Line>
        <Line>גם מצאנו שעכ"פ צריכים השמונה פרנסים והארבעה הנותרים כשירים זה לזה לגמרי, כמו שהיו השנים עשר פרנסים עד היום הזה כשירים על פי האופנים המבוארי'</Line>
        <Line>בפשר הנ"ל בפנקס הנ"ל. הנלע"ד כתבנו וחתמנו, יום ב', ח"י אלול תכ"א לפ"ק.</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <List type="signatures">
        <Item>
          <Line>נאום מנחם מענדל ר' יצחק ר' אביגדורש זצ"ל ה"ה חונה פה ק"ק ורנקבורט</Line>
        </Item>
        <Item>
          <Line>ונאום יצחק בר אהרן ז"ל נייברג</Line>
        </Item>
        <Item>
          <Line>ונאום נתן בן הגאון מהר"ר שמעון הכהן זלה"ה</Line>
        </Item>
        <Item>
          <Line>ונאום הק' משה בר נפתלי הכהן ז"ל</Line>
        </Item>
      </List>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>גם מצאנו כשיבא הברירה השנייה לאחר כלות שלשה שנים מהיום שיצטרכו שני פרנסים להיות חוץ</Line>
        <Line>מהחברותא כמשמעות התיקון ט"ו אנשים, אזי אין צריכין להיות אותן שני פרנסים מן השמונה</Line>
        <Line>פרנסים דוקא רק יכולין להיות מן הד' אנשים הנותרים. כ"ד יום הנ"ל.</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <List type="signatures_addendum">
        <Item>
          <Line>ונאום הק' מאיר שטערן</Line>
        </Item>
        <Item>
          <Line>נאום מנחם מענדל הנ"ל</Line>
        </Item>
        <Item>
          <Line>ונאום יצחק נייברג</Line>
        </Item>
        <Item>
          <Line>ונאום נתן הנ"ל</Line>
        </Item>
        <Item>
          <Line>ונאום משה הנ"ל</Line>
        </Item>
        <Item>
          <Line>ונאום מאיר הנ"ל</Line>
        </Item>
      </List>
    </Body>
  </Page>
</HistoricalDocument>

    <Body>
      <Heading type="other">
        <Line>
          <Initial type="simple">ז</Initial>
        </Line>
      </Heading>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>זמן מה קודם ברירות הפרנסים מחויבים הפרנסים להכריז על ידי שמש הקהלה</Line>
        <Line>באחד מיום הכניסה בחרם נידוי ושמת' שלא יעשה שום אדם קנוניא יהיה מי שיהי'</Line>
        <Line>בברירת הפרנסים בלי שום ערמה ותחבולה מי יכתוב לפרנס או מי לא יכתוב לפרנס</Line>
        <Line>גם לא ידבר שום אדם עם מי שיקרא לכתוב הפרנסים את מי יכתוב ומי לא יכתוב ומי</Line>
        <Line>שראוי לכתוב אותו לפרנס יהיה התיקון כמקדם שתיקנו ט"ו אנשים שנת תי"ח לפ"ק דהיינו</Line>
        <Line>איין בעל בית דש אחד מאבותיו איז מקהלתינו דערף ניט זיין אלש ל"ה שנים אלט זיין</Line>
        <Line>שיהיה ראוי להיות פרנס הקהלה אבר וועלכר קיינר מאבותיו מקהילתנו איז, מוז ארבעי'</Line>
        <Line>שנים אלט זיין ווען ער זאל מיגן מבורר ווערדן להיות פרנס קהילתינו וכל הנ"ל מחויב</Line>
        <Line>לקיים הגבאי בעונש חרם</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Heading type="other">
        <Line>
          <Initial type="simple">ח</Initial>
        </Line>
      </Heading>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>ברירת הפרנסים יהיה באופן זה דהיינו תמוז תל"ו לפ"ק דיא ך' בעלי בתים דיא</Line>
        <Line>פרנסים שרייבן הרשות בידם לכתוב מי שירצו מיגן י"ב אנדרה פרנסים</Line>
        <Line>שרייבן אכן ב' פרנסים מוזן זיא לפחות אויז דען פרנסות לאזן וועלכי דש ווינגשטי</Line>
        <Line>דעות האבן אונטר דיא פרנסים זאלין הג' שנים אויז דעם פרנסות בלייבן והשני</Line>
        <Line>בעלי בתים דיא הרוב דיעות אונטר דיא בעלי בתים האבן הגם זיא האבן ווינגר</Line>
        <Line>דעות אלש דיא שני פרנסים בכל זאת זאלין השני בעלי בתים במקום הפרנסים זיין</Line>
        <Line>זוא ח"ו פרנס אחד קודם הברירה נעדר ווער בכל זאת זאל מן ב' פרנסים הויסן לאזן</Line>
        <Line>אכן באם יעדרו שנים ח"ו קודם הברירה זאל רק פרנס אחד מוזן הויסן בלייבן</Line>
        <Line>וחודש ימים קודם ברירת הפרנסים דהיינו תמוז שנת תל"ט וגם בשנת תמ"ב מחויבי'</Line>
        <Line>הפרנסים בחומר חרם הנ"ל להתאסף מ' בעלי בתים עיקרי הקהלה להחברות' להתייעץ</Line>
        <Line>יחד מה לעשות בענייני ברירות הפרנסים דהיינו אוב מן זאל ווידר ב' או אחד או</Line>
        <Line>גר קייני הויסן צו לאזן אודר ווידר בוחר צו זיין ט"ו אנשים מיט ג' ביקסן כנ"ל להתיעץ</Line>
        <Line>איזה דרך ישכון אור ברירת הפרנסים הנ"ל אכן דוקא אין דען פונקטן ולא בשום דבר אחר</Line>
        <Line>כי כל מה שתיקנו הט"ו אנשים הנקובי' בשמות בשולי היריעה זאל אלש בכל תוקף ועוז בלייבן</Line>
        <Line>ואצל ברירת הפרנסים יהיה באב"ד ועוד זאל מן יו"ד דיא גרעסטן זקנים בוחר זיין הראוים</Line>
        <Line>לכך אשר יהיו בימים ההם אונ' זיא בקלפי ווארפן אונ' ה' דר פון ארויז נעמן היודעים ומכירי'</Line>
        <Line>בני קהלתינו דש מן קיין פסולים שרייבט ודוקא ה' זקנים ואין להם רשות ליקח יותר יהיה מי</Line>
        <Line>שיהיה ואותן ה' זקנים מחויבי' להגיד לכל אחד ואחד מהכ"ף אנשים דיא פרנסי' שרייבן</Line>
        <Line>דש זיא מוזן ב' פרנסים הויסן לאזן אונ' שני בעלי בתים במקומם שרייבן ואף אם</Line>
        <Line>נעדר אחד ח"ו מהפרנסים בכל זאת זאלין זיא ב' פרנסים הויסן לאזן רק אם יעדרו שני</Line>
        <Line>פרנסים ח"ו זאלין זיא פרנס אחד הויסן לאזן כל אלו הדברים יאמרו ויגידו להכ"ף</Line>
        <Line>אנשים קודם הכתיבה ואותן ה' אנשים דיא דר בייא זיצין אצל ברירת הפרנסים דערפין</Line>
        <Line>ניט נבחר לפרנסים ווערדן דיא ך' בעלי בתים דיא פרנסים מברר זיין תכף ומייד דש</Line>
        <Line>ער דש צעטלכן פון י"ב פרנסים בשרייבן האט זאל ער מחויב זיין תכף דיא ט' אנשים</Line>
        <Line>צו שרייבן מקדם ער בבית הכנסת החדשה גיט אונ' דש צעטליכן זאל בקלפי מיוחד</Line>
        <Line>גליגט ווערדן והך' בעלי בתים שיכתבו הפרנסי' כנ"ל זאלין קיין פסולים מחמת קורבה או ג' מחותנים</Line>
        <Line>שרייבן מפני תיקון הקדמונים וכל הנ"ל יקוים בעונש חרם חמור</Line>
      </Paragraph>
    </Body>
  </Page>
</HistoricalDocument>

<HistoricalDocument xmlns="http://example.com/historicaldocument">
  <Metadata>
    <Language>Hebrew</Language>
    <WritingDirection>rtl</WritingDirection>
    <PhysicalDescription>Medieval Hebrew manuscript page, parchment with brown ink, showing a two-column layout with marginal notations</PhysicalDescription>
    <Description>Biblical text from Deuteronomy, showing chapters 23-25</Description>
    <Script>Hebrew</Script>
  </Metadata>
  <Page>
    <Header>
      <PageNumber>96</PageNumber>
    </Header>
    <Body>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>מוצא שפתיך תשמר ועשית כאשר</Line>
        <Line>נדרת ליהוה אלהיך נדבה אשר דברת</Line>
        <Line>בפיך ˙ : כי תבא בכרם רעך</Line>
        <Line>ואכלת ענבים כנפשך שבעך ואל כליך</Line>
        <Line>לא תתן : כי תבא בקמת רעך</Line>
        <Line>וקטפת מלילת בידך וחרמש</Line>
        <Line>לא תניף על קמת רעך : כי יקח</Line>
        <Line>איש אשה ובעלה והיה אם לא תמצא</Line>
        <Line>חן בעיניו כי מצא בה ערות דבר וכתב</Line>
        <Line>לה ספר כריתת ונתן בידה ושלחה</Line>
        <Line>מביתו : ויצאה מביתו והלכה והיתה</Line>
        <Line>לאיש אחר : ושנאה האיש האחרון</Line>
        <Line>וכתב לה ספר כריתת ונתן בידה ושלחה</Line>
        <Line>מביתו או כי ימות האיש האחרון אשר</Line>
        <Line>לקחה לו לאשה : לא יוכל בעלה הראשון</Line>
        <Line>אשר שלחה לשוב לקחתה להיות לו</Line>
        <Line>לאשה אחרי אשר הטמאה כי תועבה</Line>
        <Line>הוא לפני יהוה ולא תחטיא את הארץ</Line>
        <Line>אשר יהוה אלהיך נתן לך נחלה :</Line>
        <Line>כי יקח איש אשה חדשה</Line>
        <Line>לא יצא בצבא ולא יעבר עליו לכל</Line>
        <Line>דבר נקי יהיה לביתו שנה אחת ושמח</Line>
        <Line>את אשתו אשר לקח : לא יחבל רחים</Line>
        <Line>ורכב כי נפש הוא חבל ˙ : כי</Line>
        <Line>ימצא איש גנב נפש מאחיו מבני ישראל</Line>
        <Line>והתעמר בו ומכרו ומת הגנב ההוא</Line>
        <Line>ובערת הרע מקרבך :</Line>
        <Line>השמר בנגע הצרעת לשמר מאד</Line>
        <Line>ולעשות ככל אשר יורו אתכם הכהנים</Line>
        <Line>הלוים כאשר צויתם תשמרו לעשות :</Line>
        <Line>זכור את אשר עשה יהוה אלהיך למרים</Line>
        <Line>בדרך בצאתכם ממצרים :</Line>
        <Line>כי תשה ברעך משאת מאומה</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>לא תבא אל ביתו לעבט עבטו : בחוץ</Line>
        <Line>תעמד והאיש אשר אתה נשה בו יוציא</Line>
        <Line>אליך את העבוט החוצה : ואם איש</Line>
        <Line>עני הוא לא תשכב בעבטו : השב תשיב</Line>
        <Line>לו את העבוט כבוא השמש ושכב</Line>
        <Line>בשלמתו וברכך ולך תהיה צדקה לפני</Line>
        <Line>יהוה אלהיך ˙ : לא תעשק</Line>
        <Line>שכיר עני ואביון מאחיך או מגרך אשר</Line>
        <Line>בארצך בשעריך : ביומו תתן שכרו ולא</Line>
        <Line>תבוא עליו השמש כי עני הוא ואליו</Line>
        <Line>הוא נשא את נפשו ולא יקרא עליך אל</Line>
        <Line>יהוה והיה בך חטא : לא</Line>
        <Line>יומתו אבות על בנים ובנים לא יומתו על</Line>
        <Line>אבות איש בחטאו יומתו :</Line>
        <Line>לא תטה משפט גר יתום ולא תחבל</Line>
        <Line>בגד אלמנה : וזכרת כי עבד היית במצרים</Line>
        <Line>ויפדך יהוה אלהיך משם על כן אנכי</Line>
        <Line>מצוך לעשות את הדבר הזה :</Line>
        <Line>כי תקצר קצירך בשדך ושכחת</Line>
        <Line>עמר בשדה לא תשוב לקחתו לגר ליתום</Line>
        <Line>ולאלמנה יהיה למען יברכך יהוה אלהיך</Line>
        <Line>בכל מעשה ידיך : כי תחבט</Line>
        <Line>זיתך לא תפאר אחריך לגר ליתום</Line>
        <Line>ולאלמנה יהיה : כי תבצר כרמך לא תעולל</Line>
        <Line>אחריך לגר ליתום ולאלמנה יהיה : וזכרת</Line>
        <Line>כי עבד היית בארץ מצרים על כן אנכי</Line>
        <Line>מצוך לעשות את הדבר הזה :</Line>
        <Line>כי יהיה ריב בין אנשים ונגשו</Line>
        <Line>אל המשפט ושפטום והצדיקו את</Line>
        <Line>הצדיק והרשיעו את הרשע : והיה אם</Line>
        <Line>בן הכות הרשע והפילו השפט והכהו</Line>
        <Line>לפניו כדי רשעתו במספר : ארבעים יכנו</Line>
        <Line>לא יסיף פן יסיף להכתו על אלה מכה</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <MarginalNote placement="bottom_margin">
        <Line>ושנאה ג׳ אל תשנא את אחיך ˙ ושנאה האיש האחרון ˙ ושנאתיה ˙ ושנאה האיש האחרון ˙ ושנאתיה ˙ ושנאה האיש האחרון ˙ ושנאתיה ˙</Line>
      </MarginalNote>
    </Body>
  </Page>
</HistoricalDocument>

<HistoricalDocument xmlns="http://example.com/historicaldocument">
  <Metadata>
    <Language>Hebrew</Language>
    <WritingDirection>rtl</WritingDirection>
    <PhysicalDescription>Parchment manuscript page with Hebrew text arranged in three columns. Page number 96 visible in top left corner.</PhysicalDescription>
    <Description>Medieval Hebrew biblical manuscript containing text from the Book of Jeremiah.</Description>
    <Script>Hebrew</Script>
  </Metadata>
  <Page>
    <Header>
      <PageNumber>96</PageNumber>
    </Header>
    <Body>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>והנביאים וכל</Line>
        <Line>העם את ירמיהו</Line>
        <Line>מדבר את הדברים</Line>
        <Line>האלה בבית</Line>
        <Line>יהוה : ויהי ככלות</Line>
        <Line>ירמיהו לדבר</Line>
        <Line>את כל אשר צוה</Line>
        <Line>יהוה לדבר אל</Line>
        <Line>כל העם ויתפשו</Line>
        <Line>אתו הכהנים</Line>
        <Line>והנביאים וכל</Line>
        <Line>העם לאמר מות</Line>
        <Line>תמות : מדוע</Line>
        <Line>נבאת בשם יהוה</Line>
        <Line>לאמר כשילוח</Line>
        <Line>יהיה הבית הזה</Line>
        <Line>והעיר הזאת</Line>
        <Line>תחרב מאין יושב</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>ויקהל כל העם</Line>
        <Line>אל ירמיהו בבית</Line>
        <Line>יהוה : וישמעו</Line>
        <Line>שרי יהודה את</Line>
        <Line>הדברים האלה</Line>
        <Line>ויעלו מבית המלך</Line>
        <Line>בית יהוה וישבו</Line>
        <Line>בפתח שער בית</Line>
        <Line>יהוה החדש :</Line>
        <Line>ויאמרו</Line>
        <Line>הכהנים והנביאים</Line>
        <Line>אל השרים ואל</Line>
        <Line>כל העם לאמר</Line>
        <Line>משפט מות לאיש</Line>
        <Line>הזה כי נבא אל</Line>
        <Line>העיר הזאת כאשר</Line>
        <Line>שמעתם באזניכם :</Line>
        <Line>ויאמר ירמיהו</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>אל כל השרים</Line>
        <Line>ואל כל העם</Line>
        <Line>לאמר יהוה שלחני</Line>
        <Line>להנבא אל הבית</Line>
        <Line>הזה ואל העיר</Line>
        <Line>הזאת את כל</Line>
        <Line>הדברים אשר</Line>
        <Line>שמעתם : ועתה</Line>
        <Line>היטיבו דרכיכם</Line>
        <Line>ומעלליכם ושמעו</Line>
        <Line>בקול יהוה</Line>
        <Line>אלהיכם וינחם</Line>
        <Line>יהוה אל הרעה</Line>
        <Line>אשר דבר אליכם :</Line>
        <Line>ואני הנני בידכם</Line>
        <Line>עשו לי כטוב</Line>
        <Line>וכישר בעיניכם :</Line>
        <Line>אך ידע תדעו כי</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <MarginalNote placement="top_margin">
        <Line>אמר אלהים ׃ אשר גליתי אתכם שמה ׃ ובאו ושמעו אמרי אדני יהוה ׃ ושמעו אמרי אדני יהוה ׃ ושמעו אמרי אדני יהוה ׃</Line>
      </MarginalNote>
      <MarginalNote placement="bottom_margin">
        <Line>ויאמר ירמיהו אל כל השרים ואל כל העם לאמר יהוה שלחני להנבא אל הבית הזה ואל העיר הזאת את כל הדברים אשר שמעתם ׃ ועתה היטיבו דרכיכם ומעלליכם ושמעו בקול יהוה אלהיכם וינחם יהוה אל הרעה אשר דבר אליכם ׃ ואני הנני בידכם עשו לי כטוב וכישר בעיניכם ׃</Line>
      </MarginalNote>
    </Body>
  </Page>

<HistoricalDocument xmlns="http://example.com/historicaldocument">
  <Metadata>
    <Language>Hebrew</Language>
    <WritingDirection>rtl</WritingDirection>
    <PhysicalDescription>Medieval Hebrew manuscript, parchment, two pages visible showing multiple columns of text</PhysicalDescription>
    <Description>Biblical text from Kings II (Melachim II), containing the story of Naaman, Gehazi, and Elisha</Description>
    <Script>Hebrew</Script>
  </Metadata>
  <Page>
    <Header>
      <PageNumber>124</PageNumber>
    </Header>
    <Body>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>גדול הנביא דבר אליך הלוא</Line>
        <Line>תעשה ואף כי אמר אליך</Line>
        <Line>רחץ וטהר : וירד ויטבל</Line>
        <Line>בירדן שבע פעמים כדבר</Line>
        <Line>איש האלהים וישב בשרו</Line>
        <Line>כבשר נער קטן ויטהר : וישב</Line>
        <Line>אל איש האלהים הוא וכל</Line>
        <Line>מחנהו ויבא ויעמד לפניו</Line>
        <Line>ויאמר הנה נא ידעתי כי אין</Line>
        <Line>אלהים בכל הארץ כי אם</Line>
        <Line>בישראל ועתה קח נא ברכה</Line>
        <Line>מאת עבדך : ויאמר חי יהוה</Line>
        <Line>אשר עמדתי לפניו אם אקח</Line>
        <Line>ויפצר בו לקחת וימאן : ויאמר</Line>
        <Line>נעמן ולא יתן נא לעבדך</Line>
        <Line>משא צמד פרדים אדמה כי</Line>
        <Line>לוא יעשה עוד עבדך עלה</Line>
        <Line>וזבח לאלהים אחרים כי אם</Line>
        <Line>ליהוה : לדבר הזה יסלח</Line>
        <Line>יהוה לעבדך בבוא אדני בית</Line>
        <Line>רמון להשתחות שמה והוא</Line>
        <Line>נשען על ידי והשתחויתי בית</Line>
        <Line>רמן בהשתחויתי בית רמן</Line>
        <Line>יסלח נא יהוה לעבדך בדבר</Line>
        <Line>הזה : ויאמר לו לך לשלום</Line>
        <Line>וילך מאתו כברת ארץ :</Line>
        <Line>ויאמר גיחזי נער</Line>
        <Line>אלישע איש האלהים הנה</Line>
        <Line>חשך אדני את נעמן הארמי</Line>
        <Line>הזה מקחת מידו את אשר</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>הביא חי יהוה כי אם רצתי</Line>
        <Line>אחריו ולקחתי מאתו מאומה :</Line>
        <Line>וירדף גיחזי אחרי נעמן</Line>
        <Line>ויראה נעמן רץ אחריו ויפל</Line>
        <Line>מעל המרכבה לקראתו</Line>
        <Line>ויאמר השלום : ויאמר שלום</Line>
        <Line>אדני שלחני לאמר הנה עתה</Line>
        <Line>זה באו אלי שני נערים מהר</Line>
        <Line>אפרים מבני הנביאים תנה</Line>
        <Line>נא להם ככר כסף ושתי</Line>
        <Line>חלפות בגדים : ויאמר נעמן</Line>
        <Line>הואל קח ככרים ויפרץ בו</Line>
        <Line>ויצר ככרים כסף בשני</Line>
        <Line>חרטים ושתי חלפות בגדים</Line>
        <Line>ויתן אל שני נעריו וישאו</Line>
        <Line>לפניו : ויבא אל העפל ויקח</Line>
        <Line>מידם ויפקד בבית וישלח</Line>
        <Line>את האנשים וילכו : והוא בא</Line>
        <Line>ויעמד אל אדניו ויאמר אליו</Line>
        <Line>אלישע מאן גחזי ויאמר</Line>
        <Line>לא הלך עבדך אנה ואנה :</Line>
        <Line>ויאמר אליו לא לבי</Line>
        <Line>הלך כאשר הפך איש מעל</Line>
        <Line>מרכבתו לקראתך העת</Line>
        <Line>לקחת את הכסף ולקחת</Line>
        <Line>בגדים וזיתים וכרמים וצאן</Line>
        <Line>ובקר ועבדים ושפחות :</Line>
        <Line>וצרעת נעמן תדבק בך ובזרעך</Line>
        <Line>לעולם ויצא מלפניו מצרע</Line>
        <Line>כשלג : ויאמרו</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>בני הנביאים אל אלישע הנה</Line>
        <Line>נא המקום אשר אנחנו ישבים</Line>
        <Line>שם לפניך צר ממנו : נלכה</Line>
        <Line>נא עד הירדן ונקחה משם</Line>
        <Line>איש קורה אחת ונעשה לנו</Line>
        <Line>שם מקום לשבת שם ויאמר</Line>
        <Line>לכו : ויאמר האחד הואל נא</Line>
        <Line>ולך את עבדיך ויאמר אני</Line>
        <Line>אלך : וילך אתם ויבאו הירדנה</Line>
        <Line>ויגזרו העצים : ויהי האחד</Line>
        <Line>מפיל הקורה ואת הברזל נפל</Line>
        <Line>אל המים ויצעק ויאמר אהה</Line>
        <Line>אדני והוא שאול : ויאמר איש</Line>
        <Line>האלהים אנה נפל ויראהו</Line>
        <Line>את המקום ויקצב עץ וישלך</Line>
        <Line>שמה ויצף הברזל : ויאמר</Line>
        <Line>הרם לך וישלח ידו ויקחהו :</Line>
        <Line>ומלך ארם היה נלחם</Line>
        <Line>בישראל ויועץ אל עבדיו</Line>
        <Line>לאמר אל מקום פלני אלמני</Line>
        <Line>תחנתי : וישלח איש האלהים</Line>
        <Line>אל מלך ישראל לאמר השמר</Line>
        <Line>מעבר המקום הזה כי שם</Line>
        <Line>ארם נחתים : וישלח מלך</Line>
        <Line>ישראל אל המקום אשר</Line>
        <Line>אמר לו איש האלהים</Line>
        <Line>והזהירה ונשמר שם לא</Line>
        <Line>אחת ולא שתים : ויסער לב</Line>
        <Line>מלך ארם על הדבר הזה</Line>
        <Line>ויקרא אל עבדיו ויאמר</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>אליהם הלוא תגידו לי מי</Line>
        <Line>משלנו אל מלך ישראל :</Line>
        <Line>ויאמר אחד מעבדיו</Line>
        <Line>לוא אדני המלך כי אלישע הנביא</Line>
        <Line>אשר בישראל יגיד למלך</Line>
        <Line>ישראל את הדברים אשר</Line>
        <Line>תדבר בחדר משכבך : ויאמר</Line>
        <Line>לכו וראו איכה הוא ואשלח</Line>
        <Line>ואקחהו ויגד לו לאמר הנה</Line>
        <Line>בדתן : וישלח שמה סוסים</Line>
        <Line>ורכב וחיל כבד ויבאו לילה</Line>
        <Line>ויקפו על העיר : וישכם משרת</Line>
        <Line>איש האלהים לקום ויצא</Line>
        <Line>והנה חיל סובב את העיר</Line>
        <Line>וסוס ורכב ויאמר נערו אליו</Line>
        <Line>אהה אדני איכה נעשה : ויאמר</Line>
        <Line>אל תירא כי רבים אשר אתנו</Line>
        <Line>מאשר אותם : ויתפלל אלישע</Line>
        <Line>ויאמר יהוה פקח נא את עיניו</Line>
        <Line>ויראה ויפקח יהוה את עיני</Line>
        <Line>הנער וירא והנה ההר מלא</Line>
        <Line>סוסים ורכב אש סביבת אלישע :</Line>
        <Line>וירדו אליו ויתפלל אלישע</Line>
        <Line>אל יהוה ויאמר הך נא את</Line>
        <Line>הגוי הזה בסנורים ויכם בסנורים כדבר</Line>
        <Line>אלישע : ויאמר אלהם אלישע</Line>
        <Line>לא זה הדרך ולא זה העיר</Line>
        <Line>לכו אחרי ואוליכה אתכם אל</Line>
        <Line>האיש אשר תבקשון וילך</Line>
        <Line>אותם שמרונה : ויהי כבאם</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>שמרון ויאמר אלישע יהוה</Line>
        <Line>פקח את עיני אלה ויראו</Line>
        <Line>ויפקח יהוה את עיניהם</Line>
        <Line>ויראו והנה בתוך שמרון :</Line>
        <Line>ויאמר מלך ישראל אל</Line>
        <Line>אלישע כראתו אתם האכה</Line>
        <Line>אכה אבי : ויאמר לא תכה</Line>
        <Line>האשר שבית בחרבך ובקשתך</Line>
        <Line>אתה מכה שים לחם ומים</Line>
        <Line>לפניהם ויאכלו וישתו וילכו</Line>
        <Line>אל אדניהם : ויכרה להם כרה</Line>
        <Line>גדולה ויאכלו וישתו וישלחם</Line>
        <Line>וילכו אל אדניהם ולא יספו</Line>
        <Line>עוד גדודי ארם לבוא בארץ</Line>
        <Line>ישראל : ויהי</Line>
        <Line>אחרי כן ויקבץ בן הדד מלך</Line>
        <Line>ארם את כל מחנהו ויעל ויצר</Line>
        <Line>על שמרון : ויהי רעב גדול</Line>
        <Line>בשמרון והנה צרים עליה</Line>
        <Line>עד היות ראש חמור בשמנים</Line>
        <Line>כסף ורבע הקב חרייונים</Line>
        <Line>בחמשה כסף : ויהי מלך</Line>
        <Line>ישראל עבר על החמה ואשה</Line>
        <Line>צעקה אליו לאמר הושיעה</Line>
        <Line>אדני המלך : ויאמר אל יושעך</Line>
        <Line>יהוה מאין אושיעך המן הגרן</Line>
        <Line>או מן היקב : ויאמר לה המלך</Line>
        <Line>מה לך ותאמר האשה הזאת</Line>
        <Line>אמרה אלי תני את בנך</Line>
        <Line>ונאכלנו היום ואת בני נאכל</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>מחר : ונבשל את בני ונאכלהו</Line>
        <Line>ואמר אליה ביום האחר תני</Line>
        <Line>את בנך ונאכלנו ותחבא את</Line>
        <Line>בנה : ויהי כשמע המלך את</Line>
        <Line>דברי האשה ויקרע את בגדיו</Line>
        <Line>והוא עבר על החמה וירא</Line>
        <Line>העם והנה השק על בשרו</Line>
        <Line>מבית : ויאמר כה יעשה לי</Line>
        <Line>אלהים וכה יוסף אם יעמד</Line>
        <Line>ראש אלישע בן שפט עליו</Line>
        <Line>היום : ואלישע ישב בביתו</Line>
        <Line>והזקנים ישבים אתו וישלח</Line>
        <Line>איש מלפניו בטרם יבא</Line>
        <Line>המלאך אליו והוא אמר אל</Line>
        <Line>הזקנים הראיתם כי שלח בן</Line>
        <Line>המרצח הזה להסיר את</Line>
        <Line>ראשי ראו כבא המלאך</Line>
        <Line>סגרו הדלת ולחצתם אתו</Line>
        <Line>בדלת הלוא קול רגלי אדניו</Line>
        <Line>אחריו : עודנו מדבר עמם</Line>
        <Line>והנה המלאך ירד אליו</Line>
        <Line>ויאמר הנה זאת הרעה מאת</Line>
        <Line>יהוה מה אוחיל ליהוה עוד :</Line>
        <Line>ויאמר אלישע</Line>
        <Line>שמעו דבר יהוה כה אמר</Line>
        <Line>יהוה כעת מחר סאה סלת</Line>
        <Line>בשקל וסאתים שערים</Line>
        <Line>בשקל בשער שמרון : ויען</Line>
        <Line>השליש אשר למלך נשען</Line>
        <Line>על ידו את איש האלהים</Line>
      </Paragraph>
    </Body>
  </Page>
</HistoricalDocument>

The beginning of the history of Indonesia coincides with the oldest evidence of the presence of Hindu culture in that area, that is about the fifth century A.D., nevertheless we have also to consult prehistoric evidences. Moreover, since at present several regions in the archipelago remain little affected by the civilizations from abroad—Hinduism, Islam, Chinese and European in particular—these archaic communities could supply us with valuable pieces of information. Of course, this source material should be used with prudence.

This study is an attempt to present the economic structure and the economic processes as they were administered during its earliest history. Although confined in time as well as in subject, we will treat it in a larger context of “history and sociology”.

After almost a century of scholarly study of Indonesian history, linguistics, epigraphy, we may wonder that apart from political history, art and literature, only a few contributions to the economic and administrative history of hinduized Indonesia are available. This is the more surprising since our main sources, Old Javanese inscriptions, are for the greater part concerned with land tenure. These praśastis,—deeds of land grants—are understandably valuable in particular for our knowledge of the just mentioned aspects of history.

Progress was first made on the economic side by B. Schrieke, followed by J. C. van Leur, M. A. P. Meilink-Roelofsz, P. Wheatley and C. W. Wolters. But on the administrative history of ancient Java we still lack such comprehensive studies.

When I was invited to contribute to this “Handbuch” on the part of Economic and Administrative History of Early Indonesia, I was aware that I had little published material at my disposal. However, I hope that this contribution, although for the greater part based upon work in the pioneering stage and derived from primary source-material, will be useful in some respect to the interested reader.

I would like to mention here the Australian Research Grants Committee which enabled me to venture into this preliminary work and gave me an opportunity of carrying out the research on the spot in Indonesia. Here, Mr. R. Soekmono—then Director of the Archeological Institute of the Republic of Indonesia—and Mr. Amir Sutaarga, Head of the Museum Pusat, Djakarta were most helpful to me, as were their staff officers.

My gratitude also goes to Professor P. J. Worsley of the University of Sydney and to Mr. A. J. Mc. Kell B.A., who were kind enough to read through passages of my manuscript.

        <Line>On Thursday, Jas. Thompson, a mason, of Palace-</Line>

      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>Officer 448 said that about twelve o'clock on Thurs-</Line>
        <Line>day the defendant was standing in front of Bennett's</Line>
        <Line>clock, and that although repeatedly requested to</Line>
        <Line>move on he refused to do so, stating that he should</Line>
        <Line>wait until a quarter past twelve to see the figures</Line>
        <Line>Gog and Magog strike the quarter hour upon the bell.</Line>
        <Line>The consequence was that, although the street was</Line>
        <Line>not very much crowded at the moment, there was</Line>
        <Line>some obstruction caused by the obstinate refusal of</Line>

        <Line>cause the front of the Manchester Fire assurance-</Line>
        <Line>office, opposite Bennett's clock, was newly painted,</Line>
        <Line>and pedestrians ran the risk of having their clothes</Line>
        <Line>smeared.</Line>
      </Paragraph>

THE OBSTRUCTION IN CHEAPSIDE.

On Thursday, Jas. Thompson, a mason, of Palace-road, Lambeth, was brought before Mr. Alderman Lusk, at the Mansion-house, on a charge of having obstructed the thoroughfare, opposite Bennett's clock, in Cheapside.

Officer 448 said that about twelve o'clock on Thursday the defendant was standing in front of Bennett's clock, and that although repeatedly requested to move on he refused to do so, stating that he should wait until a quarter past twelve to see the figures Gog and Magog strike the quarter hour upon the bell. The consequence was that, although the street was not very much crowded at the moment, there was some obstruction caused by the obstinate refusal of the defendant to leave the spot, and this obstruction was rendered somewhat annoying to the public because the front of the Manchester Fire assurance office, opposite Bennett's clock, was newly painted, and pedestrians ran the risk of having their clothes smeared.

The prisoner said his reply to the charge was very simple. He was a mason by trade, and had made that day a holiday. He was passing along Cheapside with his wife about ten minutes after twelve o'clock, and having heard and read a good deal about Bennett's clock, and the way Gog and Magog struck the hours and quarter-hours upon the great bell, he thought he would wait until a quarter after twelve to see the figures raise their hammers and strike. The officer came up before he had been standing on the footway more than half a minute, and told him to move on, and he then walked up and down the place rather smartly. This displeased the officer, who took him off to the station-house, and booked him as a public obstructionist.

Alderman Lusk said the streets of London were in general very narrow for the accommodation of the tens of thousands of the population who had to pass through them daily on business. The defendant and everybody else should know that they were not to stand gazing and blocking up the footways. However, as this was the first case of the kind which had been brought before the court, the prisoner would be discharged; but he must bear in mind that his misconduct was not to be repeated.

ment supervision and with private capital. [See also Gong Yixin; Empress Dowager; Zongli Yamen; Zeng Guofan; and Li Hongzhang.]

The Self-Strengthening Movement failed to increase China's military strength significantly, however. In 1884 French ambitions in Vietnam, a Chinese protectorate, sparked the Sino-French War (1884–1885). Poor coordination and leadership resulted in China's defeat. Ten years later a clash with Japan over Korea resulted in the Sino-Japanese War (1894–1895), which Japan won easily. [See also Sino-Japanese War.]

After China's defeat, a "scramble for concessions" ensued. Germany, Russia, France, and Britain all forced China to lease ports and recognize foreign spheres of influence over Chinese territory. Nominal Chinese sovereignty was preserved in the foreign areas, mainly because the competing powers checked each others' ambitions. Nonetheless, imperialist pressure threatened to destroy China's unity and independence. [See also Imperialism.]

Late Qing Reform. This crisis brought a group of reformers to the attention of the Guangxu emperor (r. 1875–1908). Their leader, Kang Youwei (1858–1927), reinterpreted Confucianism to sanction radical innovation. In the summer of 1898 the emperor issued a series of decrees calling for wide-ranging institutional reforms and economic development, but official resistance blocked implementation of the reforms. In September 1898, conservatives led by Empress Dowager Cixi staged a coup d'état. The emperor was placed under house arrest; the reformers fled into exile or were arrested.

The new conservative government soon threw its support behind the Boxers (more properly, Yihtuan, "righteous and harmonious society"), a popular movement dedicated to driving Westerners out of China. The Boxers occupied Beijing in the summer of 1900 and besieged the foreign legations with the connivance of the Qing government, which declared war on the foreign powers. Regional officials in central and southern China, however, ignored the declaration of war and maintained friendly relations with the powers. An international force occupied Beijing in August 1900. In 1901 China was forced to sign the Boxer Protocol, which provided for a foreign military presence in North China, punishment for Chinese officials implicated in the Boxer movement, and an indemnity. [See also Yihetuan.]

The chastened Qing government thereupon undertook an extensive reform program, similar in many ways to the one aborted in 1898. A new public education system was inaugurated, and in 1905 the civil service examination system, based on the Confucian classics, was abolished. The traditional Six Boards were replaced with new ministries. Modern military academies trained a new officer corps and Yuan Shikai (1859–1916) established the Beiyang Army, a modern military force.

Japan's defeat of Russia in 1905 appeared to prove the superiority of constitutionalism over autocracy. The Qing government slowly began to establish representative assemblies. Provincial assemblies, with advisory functions but not legislative powers, were established in 1909. A consultative National Assembly met the following year. Nevertheless, the Manchu princes controlling the government moved cautiously and continued to monopolize the highest positions, thereby increasing Chinese frustrations and resentment.

The Revolution of 1911. In the decade following the Boxer Rebellion, expatriate reformers and revolutionaries vied for support. Kang Youwei, in exile in Japan, remained loyal to the Qing and opposed attempts to overthrow the dynasty. His disciple Liang Qichao (1873–1929) became familiar with Western political ideas and spread them in the journals he published in Tokyo. [See also Kang Youwei and Liang Qichao.]

Their most important rival was another Chinese exile, Sun Yat-sen (1866–1925). Sun was a Western-educated Cantonese with ties to overseas Chinese communities. In 1905 Sun established a revolutionary organization based in Tokyo, the Tongmenghui (Revolutionary Alliance). He promoted republicanism and his "Three Principles of the People"—nationalism, people's rights, and people's livelihood.

On 10 October 1911 revolutionary soldiers in the Qing army garrison in Wuchang mutinied. The authority of the Qing government rapidly collapsed; provincial assemblies in southern and central China declared their independence from the Manchus, and a provisional government was established in Nanjing. Sun Yat-sen returned from a sixteen-year exile to be inaugurated as the first president of the Republic of China.

The Qing court called upon the retired general Yuan Shikai to deal with the revolutionaries. Sun offered to resign the presidency in favor of Yuan if Yuan were to support the republic. Yuan engineered the abdication of the five-year-old Xuantong emperor in February 1912, and accepted the presidency, ending China's two millennia of imperial rule.

[See also Xinhai Revolution; Xuantong Emperor; Sun Yat-sen; Yuan Shikai; and China, Republic Period.]

        <Line>THE EXAMINER.</Line>

    <Body>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>eat the dry and withered grass around us. We now lay</Line>
        <Line>down to rest ourselves, and the boy soon fell asleep ; I was</Line>
        <Line>however feverish and restless, and could not close my eyes.</Line>
        <Line>In an hour and a half I arose, got up the horses and saddled</Line>
        <Line>them, and then, awaking my companion, we again pushed</Line>
        <Line>on by moonlight. At ten miles we crossed a well‐beaten</Line>
        <Line>native pathway, plainly discernible even then, and this we</Line>
        <Line>followed down towards the cliﬀs, fully hoping it would lead</Line>
        <Line>to water. Our hopes, however, had been excited but to</Line>
        <Line>render our disappointment the greater, for upon tracing it</Line>
        <Line>onwards we found it terminate abruptly at a large circular</Line>
        <Line>hole of limestone rock, which would retain a considerable</Line>
        <Line>quantity of water after rains, but was now without a single</Line>
        <Line>drop. Gloomily turning away we again pushed on for</Line>
        <Line>eight miles further, and at three in the morning of the 10th</Line>
        <Line>were compelled to halt from downright exhaustion and</Line>
        <Line>fatigue. The horses and sheep were knocked up. The</Line>
        <Line>poor boy was so tired and sleepy that he could scarcely sit</Line>
        <Line>upon his horse, and I found myself actually dosing as I</Line>
        <Line>walked : mechanically my legs kept moving forwards, but</Line>
        <Line>my eyes were every now and then closed in forgetfulness of</Line>
        <Line>all around me, until I was suddenly thrown down by get‑</Line>
        <Line>ting entangled amongst the scrub, or aroused by a severe</Line>
        <Line>blow across the face from the recoil of a bough after the</Line>
        <Line>passage of the boy's horse. I now judged we had come</Line>
        <Line>about ninety‐three miles from Yeerkum‐ban‐kauwe, and</Line>
        <Line>hoped that we could not be very far from water. Having</Line>
        <Line>tied up the horses for an hour or two, and without making</Line>
        <Line>a ﬁre, or even unrolling our cloaks to cover us, we stretched</Line>
        <Line>ourselves on the ground, and were in a few moments fast</Line>
        <Line>asleep.</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <BlockQuotation>
        <Line>" March 10.—At ﬁve we were again on our route, every</Line>
        <Line>moment expecting to see a break in the line of cliﬀs along</Line>
        <Line>which we had now travelled so far. Alas ! they still con‑</Line>
        <Line>tinued stretching as far as the eye could see to the west‑</Line>
        <Line>ward, and as fast as we arrived at one point which had</Line>
        <Line>bounded our vision ( and beyond which we hoped a change</Line>
        <Line>might occur), it was but to be met with the view of another</Line>
        <Line>beyond. Distressing and fatal as the continuance of these</Line>
        <Line>cliﬀs might prove to us, there was a grandeur and sub‑</Line>
        <Line>limity in their appearance that was most imposing, and</Line>
        <Line>which struck me with admiration. Stretching out before</Line>
        <Line>us in lofty unbroken outline, they presented the singular</Line>
        <Line>and romantic appearance of massy battlements of masonry,</Line>
        <Line>supported by huge buttresses, and glittering in the morn‑</Line>
        <Line>ing sun which had now risen upon them, and made the</Line>
        <Line>scene beautiful even amidst the dangers and anxieties of</Line>
        <Line>our situation."</Line>
      </BlockQuotation>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>In a direct line of upwards of 800 miles thus</Line>
        <Line>gone over by Mr Eyre, there does not seem to</Line>
        <Line>have been a watercourse, or a hollow of any kind,</Line>
        <Line>crossed ; and not a drop of fresh water accessible</Line>
        <Line>on the surface. It could only be obtained by dig‑</Line>
        <Line>ging close to the sea‐shore, or the sand‐hills of the</Line>
        <Line>coast ; and even by that means was often not pro‑</Line>
        <Line>curable for distances of 160 miles together. The</Line>
        <Line>dreary waste is described by Mr Eyre as an almost</Line>
        <Line>uniform table land of fossil formation, with an ele‑</Line>
        <Line>vation of from three to ﬁve hundred feet ; covered</Line>
        <Line>for the most part by dense impenetrable scrubs,</Line>
        <Line>and only varied on its surface by occasional sandy</Line>
        <Line>or rocky undulations. The dangers and suﬀerings</Line>
        <Line>of travel in such a region may be conceived ; as</Line>
        <Line>well as its generally uninteresting character. But</Line>
        <Line>every now and then a startling little trait occurs</Line>
        <Line>which gives the living touch of reality to the scene ;</Line>
        <Line>and again carries the reader forward, watchful and</Line>
        <Line>anxious for the traveller. In the following for</Line>
        <Line>instance.</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <BlockQuotation>
        <Line>" . . . I occupied myself in writing and charting during</Line>
        <Line>the day, and at night amused myself in taking stellar obser‑</Line>
        <Line>vations for latitude. I had already taken the altitude of Vega,</Line>
        <Line>and deduced the latitude to be 32 deg. 3 min. 23 sec. S. ;</Line>
        <Line>leaving my artiﬁcial horizon on the ground outside whilst I</Line>
        <Line>remained in the tent waiting until Altair came to the meri‑</Line>
        <Line>dian, I then took my sextant and went out to observe this</Line>
        <Line>star also ; but upon putting down my hand to take hold of</Line>
        <Line>the horizon‐glass in order to wipe the dew oﬀ, my ﬁngers</Line>
        <Line>went into the quicksilver—the horizon‐glass was gone, and</Line>
        <Line>also the piece of canvas I had put on the ground to lie down</Line>
        <Line>upon whilst observing so low an altitude as that of Vega.</Line>
        <Line>Searching a little more, I missed a spade, a parcel of horse‑</Line>
        <Line>shoes, an axe, a tin dish, some ropes, a grubbing‐hoe, and</Line>
        <Line>several smaller things which had been left outside the tent,</Line>
        <Line>as not being likely to take any injury from the damp. It</Line>
        <Line>was evident I was surrounded by natives, who had stolen</Line>
        <Line>all these things during the short time I had been in my tent,</Line>
        <Line>certainly not exceeding half an hour. The night was very</Line>
        <Line>windy, and I had heard nothing ; besides, I was encamped</Line>
        <Line>in the midst of a very dense brush of large wide‐spreading</Line>
        <Line>tea‐trees and other bushes, any of which would aﬀord a</Line>
        <Line>screen for a considerable number of natives. In daylight it</Line>
        <Line>was impossible to see many yards in distance, and nothing</Line>
        <Line>could be discerned at night. . . . As soon as I</Line>
        <Line>missed my horizon‐glass, and entertained the suspicion</Line>
        <Line>of natives being about. I hurried into the tent, and</Line>
        <Line>lighting a large blue light, run with it rapidly through</Line>
        <Line>the bushes around me. The eﬀect of this was very beauti‑</Line>
        <Line>ful amidst the darkness and gloom of the woods, and for a</Line>
        <Line>great distance in every direction objects could be seen as</Line>
        <Line>well as by day : the natives, however, were gone ; and I</Line>
        <Line>could only console myself by ﬁring a couple of balls after</Line>
        <Line>them through the underwood, to warn them of the danger</Line>
        <Line>of intruding upon me again. I then put everything which</Line>
        <Line>had been left outside into the tent, and kept watch for an</Line>
        <Line>hour or two; but my visitors came no more. . . . Rising</Line>
        <Line>very early, I set to work with an axe to clear away the</Line>
        <Line>bushes from around my tent. I now discovered that the</Line>
        <Line>natives had been concealed behind a large tea‐tree not</Line>
        <Line>twenty yards from the tent : there were numerous foot‑</Line>
        <Line>marks there, and the remains of ﬁre‐sticks which they had</Line>
        <Line>brought with them, for a native rarely moves at night with‑</Line>
        <Line>out ﬁre."</Line>
      </BlockQuotation>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>Mr Eyre seems to have no hope, in spite of</Line>
        <Line>Capt. Sturt's cheering dispatches, that any inland</Line>
        <Line>sea will ever be ultimately discovered behind this</Line>
        <Line>vast unpromising table land. Can it be, he asks,</Line>
        <Line>that the whole is one immense interminable desert,</Line>
        <Line>" or an alternation of deserts and shallow lakes ?"</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>Incidental to the narrative of the expeditions</Line>
        <Line>are many illustrations of native character : but Mr</Line>
        <Line>Eyre, as we before said, has collected all his many</Line>
        <Line>years' experiences on this head into a separate</Line>
        <Line>treatise or dissertation at the close of his work.</Line>
        <Line>The reader interested in the subject will ﬁnd his</Line>
        <Line>information curious and ample. The matters</Line>
        <Line>treated of embrace not only the physical and moral</Line>
        <Line>state of the aborigines ; their habits of life, rude</Line>
        <Line>government, and social relations ; their language</Line>
        <Line>and dialects ; but also very interesting notices of</Line>
        <Line>the eﬀects of their contact with Europeans, and</Line>
        <Line>some valuable suggestions for an improvement in</Line>
        <Line>the system generally adopted towards them.</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>Our extracts are limited by our space : but to</Line>
        <Line>even readers familiar with Captain Grey's excellent</Line>
        <Line>dissertations, much of Mr Eyre's information will</Line>
        <Line>be new and original.</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Heading type="sub">
        <Line>HUSBAND AND WIFE.</Line>
      </Heading>
      <BlockQuotation>
        <Line>" Wives are considered the absolute property of the hus‑</Line>
        <Line>band, and can be given away, or exchanged, or lent, ac‑</Line>
        <Line>cording to his caprice. A husband is denominated in the</Line>
        <Line>Adelaide dialect, Yongarra, Martanya (the owner or pro‑</Line>
        <Line>prietor of a wife). Female children are betrothed usually</Line>
        <Line>from early infancy, and such arrangements are usually ad‑</Line>
        <Line>hered to ; still in many cases circumstances occur frequently</Line>
        <Line>to cause an alteration ; but if not, the girls generally go to</Line>
        <Line>live with their husbands about the age of twelve, and some‑</Line>
        <Line>times even before that. Relatives nearer than cousins are</Line>
        <Line>not allowed to marry, and this alliance does not generally</Line>
        <Line>take place Female orphans belong to the nearest male re‑</Line>
        <Line>lative, as also does a widow, instead of to the nearest male</Line>
        <Line>relative of the husband, as was found to be the case in</Line>
        <Line>Western Australia by Captain Grey. Two or three months</Line>
        <Line>generally elapse before the widow goes to another hus‑</Line>
        <Line>band ; but if the wife dies, the man takes another as soon</Line>
        <Line>as he can get one. If a woman, having young children,</Line>
        <Line>join another tribe, the children go with her ; but I am not</Line>
        <Line>aware whether they would remain permanently attached to</Line>
        <Line>that tribe or not. Brothers often barter their sisters for</Line>
        <Line>wives for themselves, but it can only be done with the</Line>
        <Line>parents' consent, or after their death. If a wife be stolen,</Line>
        <Line>war is always continued until she is given up, or another</Line>
        <Line>female in her place.</Line>
      </BlockQuotation>
      <BlockQuotation>
        <Line>" There is no ceremony connected with the undertaking</Line>
        <Line>of marriage. In those cases where I have witnessed the</Line>
        <Line>giving away of a wife, the woman was simply ordered by</Line>
        <Line>the nearest male relative in whose disposal she was, to take</Line>
        <Line>up her ' rocko,' the bag in which a female carries the eﬀects</Line>
        <Line>of her husband, and go to the man's camp to whom she had</Line>
        <Line>been given. Marriage is not looked upon as any pledge of</Line>
        <Line>chastity, indeed no such virtue is recognised. But little</Line>
        <Line>real aﬀection consequently exists between husbands and</Line>
        <Line>wives, and young men value a wife principally for her ser‑</Line>
        <Line>vices as a slave ; in fact, when asked why they are anxious</Line>
        <Line>to obtain wives, their usual reply is, that they may get</Line>
        <Line>wood, water, and food for them, and carry whatever pro‑</Line>
        <Line>perty they possess."</Line>
      </BlockQuotation>
      <Heading type="sub">
        <Line>NATIVE MODESTY.</Line>
      </Heading>
      <BlockQuotation>
        <Line>" Innate propriety of behaviour is also frequently exhi‑</Line>
        <Line>bited by the Aborigines in their natural state, in the modest</Line>
        <Line>unasuming manner in which they take their positions to</Line>
        <Line>observe what is going on, and in a total absence of any‑</Line>
        <Line>thing that is rude or oﬀensive. It is true that the reverse</Line>
        <Line>of this is also often to be met with ; but I think it will</Line>
        <Line>usually be found that it is among natives who have before</Line>
        <Line>been in contact with Europeans, or where familiarities have</Line>
        <Line>been used with them ﬁrst, or an injudicious system of treat‑</Line>
        <Line>ment has been adopted towards them.</Line>
      </BlockQuotation>
      <BlockQuotation>
        <Line>" Delicacy of feeling is not often laid to the charge of the</Line>
        <Line>Aborigines, and yet I was witness to a singular instance of</Line>
        <Line>it at King George's Sound. I was looking one evening at</Line>
        <Line>the natives dancing, and who were, as they always are on</Line>
        <Line>these occasions, in a state of complete nudity. In the</Line>
        <Line>midst of the performance, one of the natives standing by as</Line>
        <Line>a spectator, mentioned that a white woman was passing up</Line>
        <Line>the road ; and although this was some little distance away,</Line>
        <Line>and the night was tolerably dark, they all with one accord</Line>
        <Line>crossed over to the bushes where their cloaks were, put</Line>
        <Line>them on, and resumed their amusement."</Line>
      </BlockQuotation>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>Some representations of native ornaments, wea‑</Line>
        <Line>pons, and implements and works of industry, in</Line>
        <Line>this part of the book, are useful to the text.</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Heading type="main">
        <Line>THE THEATRICAL EXAMINER.</Line>
      </Heading>
      <Heading type="sub">
        <Line>HAYMARKET.</Line>
      </Heading>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>The False Mr Pope is a retired Hammersmith</Line>
        <Line>tradesman of about ﬁve feet four, with a Ramilie</Line>
        <Line>wig and tail more than half as big as himself,</Line>
        <Line>square‐cut buckram skirts, long ﬂapped white</Line>
        <Line>waistcoat, and minute three‐cornered hat, who is</Line>
        <Line>passed oﬀ by a wag of a player upon a party of</Line>
        <Line>petticoat admirers of Pope, for the celebrated au‑</Line>
        <Line>thor of the Dunciad. To fancy Mr Buckstone in</Line>
        <Line>this predicament, is to have a very clear notion of</Line>
        <Line>Mr Peake's amusing farce.</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>It is nicely presented ; with abundance of pe‑</Line>
        <Line>ruke for the gentlemen, and of hoods, clustering</Line>
        <Line>curls, cardinals, and little china, for the ladies ; and</Line>
        <Line>it perpetrates a vast many abominable jokes, which</Line>
        <Line>nobody but the actors and actresses can possibly</Line>
        <Line>be expected to laugh at. But this is the " moral."</Line>
        <Line>The ladies are in such a state of frantic foregone</Line>
        <Line>admiration of Mr Pope, that the more audacious</Line>
        <Line>the ﬂights of Mr Buckstone the wittier they are</Line>
        <Line>taken to be ; and though this is rather a danger‑</Line>
        <Line>ous experiment for a farce, the audience help it</Line>
        <Line>out with their good‐nature.</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>Indeed it would take a troublesome amount of</Line>
        <Line>the other quality to withstand Mr Buckstone's</Line>
        <Line>practical points of drollery. When he takes oﬀ</Line>
        <Line>his wig in a sudden heat, for example, and exposes</Line>
        <Line>his small bald head. Swift's mouse under a canopy</Line>
        <Line>of state is nothing to it. When he eﬀects a series</Line>
        <Line>of practical Rapes of the Lock, too, he uses the</Line>
        <Line>scissors like a true poet. And when he passes</Line>
        <Line>from doing to suﬀering, tastes the griefs as well as</Line>
        <Line>glories of fame, and is well thrashed by Mr Curll's</Line>
        <Line>chairman as he leaves the player's house,—the act</Line>
        <Line>closed with a roar. There should have been no</Line>
        <Line>second. There is nothing but stale repetition in</Line>
        <Line>the second act. The ladies retort with a practical</Line>
        <Line>joke of their own, which is much more remarkable</Line>
        <Line>for its dullness than for any more lady‐like quality.</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Heading type="sub">
        <Line>LYCEUM.</Line>
      </Heading>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>An excellent new farce was played here on Mon‑</Line>
        <Line>day night ; better than any piece of its class which</Line>
        <Line>we have seen for many a day. It has nicety of</Line>
        <Line>character, and a good broad humour. You laugh,</Line>
        <Line>and have no need to be ashamed of your mirth.</Line>
        <Line>There is neither caricature nor coarseness. We</Line>
        <Line>cannot stay to tell the plot (which is a plot, and</Line>
        <Line>not told without some pains), but must brieﬂy</Line>
        <Line>counsel the playgoer to see Peter Jenkins. Mr</Line>
        <Line>and Mrs Keeley, Mr Wigan and Mr Meadows,</Line>
        <Line>complete an admirable cast. Mr Keeley is not</Line>
        <Line>only an honest truth‐telling fellow forced to tell</Line>
        <Line>lies for a friend ; but a conﬁrmed little bachelor,</Line>
        <Line>caught, willy‐nilly, in the snares of matrimony.</Line>
        <Line>His dilemmas are intense, and he does justice to</Line>
        <Line>them.</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Heading type="main">
        <Line>FOREIGN NEWS.</Line>
      </Heading>
      <Heading type="sub">
        <Line>FRANCE.</Line>
      </Heading>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>DEATH OF M. ROYER COLLARD.—This illustrious</Line>
        <Line>citizen died on the 4th inst., at his estate at Chateauvieux,</Line>
        <Line>near Saint‐Aignan, in the 82nd year of his age. M.</Line>
        <Line>Royer Collard had been President of the Chamber of De‑</Line>
        <Line>puties, Member of the French Academy, and Professor of</Line>
        <Line>Philosophy at the College of France.</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>THE SLAVE TRADE CONVENTION.—" The vessels in‑</Line>
        <Line>tended to act against the slave trade are not," says the</Line>
        <Line>' Constitutionnel,' " yet ready to proceed to the coasts of</Line>
        <Line>Africa. They are not to set out for six weeks or two</Line>
        <Line>months. Meanwhile communications are exchanged with</Line>
        <Line>England every day on the subject of the mission which</Line>
        <Line>the two navies are to fulﬁl together. Recently the Ad‑</Line>
        <Line>miralty has drawn up regulations for day and night sig‑</Line>
        <Line>nals, which the English and French cruisers are to make</Line>
        <Line>use of, in order to mutually recognise each other. It ap‑</Line>
        <Line>pears that we have approved of all the dispositions of</Line>
        <Line>these regulations. It is divided into two parts ; the ﬁrst</Line>
        <Line>concerning sailing vessels, and the other steamers. The</Line>
        <Line>English navy has been long occupied for its own use with</Line>
        <Line>a regulation of this kind for steamers, collisions of which</Line>
        <Line>are both frequent and dangerous. In France, nothing</Line>
        <Line>has been done in that respect."</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>RUMOURED RETIREMENT OF MARSHAL SOULT.—A</Line>
        <Line>letter from Castres announces that the Marquis de Mor‑</Line>
        <Line>nay has just arrived at Soultberg. If report can be be‑</Line>
        <Line>lieved, the marquis, who was at Beauvais for the Council‑</Line>
        <Line>General, quitted that town precipitately, in consequence</Line>
        <Line>of a pressing invitation from the Minister of War. The</Line>
        <Line>old marshal, who declares himself exceedingly fatigued</Line>
        <Line>with the struggles and diﬃculties which he has to en‑</Line>
        <Line>counter, particularly from Algeria, and who is besides</Line>
        <Line>tormented with a chronic cough, again talks of withdraw‑</Line>
        <Line>ing from oﬃce ; but, as to withdraw at his age is to give</Line>
        <Line>up public aﬀairs for ever, he is unwilling, he says, to</Line>
        <Line>take such a determination without consulting his family.</Line>
        <Line>The ' France ' discredits the report of the Marshal's</Line>
        <Line>retirement.</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>VISIT OF THE FRENCH PRINCES TO THE QUEEN OF</Line>
        <Line>SPAIN.—On the 3rd inst., the Duke and Duchess de Ne‑</Line>
        <Line>mours and the Duke d'Aumale, after visiting Biarritz</Line>
        <Line>and St Jean de Luz, arrived at the bridge which unites</Line>
        <Line>France with Spain. There the Princes alighted from</Line>
        <Line>their carriages and crossed the bridge on foot, accompa‑</Line>
        <Line>nied by Count Bresson, the French Ambassador, the Pre‑</Line>
        <Line>fect of the Department of the Lower Pyrenees ; M. Aze‑</Line>
        <Line>vedo ; Gen. Boyer, Aid‐de‐Camp of the Duke de Ne‑</Line>
        <Line>mours ; Col. Jamin, Aid‐de‐Camp of the Duke d'Aumale,</Line>
        <Line>&c. On reaching the Spanish territory they were com‑</Line>
        <Line>plimented by the Duke de San Carlos, a nobleman of the</Line>
        <Line>Queen's Bedchamber, and Senor Arana, Master of the</Line>
        <Line>Ceremonies of the Palace, in the name of the Queen, and</Line>
        <Line>by Senors Olozabal and Aldamar, in that of the province</Line>
        <Line>of Guipuzcoa. Gen. Barrenechea, commander of the pro‑</Line>
        <Line>vince, received the French Princes at the head of the</Line>
        <Line>troops with all the honours due to their rank. The people,</Line>
        <Line>on their side, loudly cheered them. The august party</Line>
        <Line>slept at Tolosa, and entered Pampeluna on the following</Line>
        <Line>day. Accounts from Bayonne of the 8th state that they</Line>
        <Line>had returned to that town in good health, highly satisﬁed</Line>
        <Line>with the reception given them, not only at Pampeluna,</Line>
        <Line>but along the whole of their journey in Spain. The Duke</Line>
        <Line>d Aumale travelled back through the valley of Bastan on</Line>
        <Line>horseback.</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>FUTURE RESIDENCE OF DON CARLOS.—The ' Consti‑</Line>
        <Line>tutionnel ' says :—" The Marquis de Villafranca is hourly</Line>
        <Line>expected at Paris. He comes to solicit, it is said, autho‑</Line>
        <Line>risation for Don Carlos and the Princess to proceed to</Line>
        <Line>Rome, the climate of Bourges being injurious to the health</Line>
        <Line>of the Princess, who was born in Brazil. If M. de</Line>
        <Line>Villafranca does not obtain passports for Italy, he is</Line>

down to rest ourselves, and the boy soon fell asleep; I was
however feverish and restless, and could not close my eyes.
In an hour and a half I arose, got up the horses and saddled
them, and then, awaking my companion, we again pushed
on by moonlight. At ten miles we crossed a well-beaten
native pathway, plainly discernible even then, and this we
followed down towards the cliffs, fully hoping it would lead
to water. Our hopes, however, had been excited but to
render our disappointment the greater, for upon tracing it
onwards we found it terminate abruptly at a large circular
hole of limestone rock, which would retain a considerable
quantity of water after rains, but was now without a single
drop. Gloomily turning away we again pushed on for
eight miles further, and at three in the morning of the 10th
were compelled to halt from downright exhaustion and
fatigue. The horses and sheep were knocked up. The
poor boy was so tired and sleepy that he could scarcely sit
upon his horse, and I found myself actually dozing as I
walked: mechanically my legs kept moving forwards, but
my eyes were every now and then closed in forgetfulness of
all around me, until I was suddenly thrown down by get-
ting entangled amongst the scrub, or aroused by a severe
blow across the face from the recoil of a bough after the
passage of the boy's horse. I now judged we had come
about ninety-three miles from Yeerkum-ban-kauwe, and
hoped that we could not be very far from water. Having
tied up the horses for an hour or two, and without making
a fire, or even unrolling our cloaks to cover us, we stretched
ourselves on the ground, and were in a few moments fast
asleep.
"March 10.—At five we were again on our route, every
moment expecting to see a break in the line of cliffs along
which we had now travelled so far. Alas! they still con-
tinued stretching as far as the eye could see to the west-
ward, and as fast as we arrived at one point which had
bounded our vision (and beyond which we hoped a change
might occur), it was but to be met with the view of another
beyond. Distressing and fatal as the continuance of these
cliffs might prove to us, there was a grandeur and sub-
limity in their appearance that was most imposing, and
which struck me with admiration. Stretching out before
us in lofty unbroken outline, they presented the singular
and romantic appearance of massive battlements of masonry,
supported by huge buttresses, and glittering in the morn-
ing sun which had now risen upon them, and made the
scene beautiful even amidst the dangers and anxieties of
our situation."
In a direct line of upwards of 800 miles thus
gone over by Mr Eyre, there does not seem to
have been a watercourse, or a hollow of any kind,
crossed; and not a drop of fresh water accessible
on the surface. It could only be obtained by dig-
ging close to the sea-shore, or the sand-hills of the
coast; and even by that means was often not pro-
curable for distances of 160 miles together. The
dreary waste is described by Mr Eyre as an almost
uniform table land of fossil formation, with an ele-
vation of from three to five hundred feet; covered
for the most part by dense impenetrable scrubs,
and only varied on its surface by occasional sandy
or rocky undulations. The dangers and sufferings
of travel in such a region may be conceived; as
well as its generally uninteresting character. But
every now and then a startling little trait occurs
which gives the living touch of reality to the scene;
and again carries the reader forward, watchful and
anxious for the traveller. In the following for
instance.
" . . . I occupied myself in writing and charting during
the day, and at night amused myself in taking stellar obser-
vations for latitude. I had already taken the altitude of Vega,
and deduced the latitude to be 32 deg. 3 min. 23 sec. S.;
leaving my artificial horizon on the ground outside whilst I
remained in the tent waiting until Altair came to the meri-
dian, I then took my sextant and went out to observe this
star also; but upon putting down my hand to take hold of
the horizon-glass in order to wipe the dew off, my fingers
went into the quicksilver—the horizon-glass was gone, and
also the piece of canvas I had put on the ground to lie down
upon whilst observing so low an altitude as that of Vega.
Searching a little more, I missed a spade, a parcel of horse-
shoes, an axe, a tin dish, some ropes, a grubbing-hoe, and
several smaller things which had been left outside the tent,
as not being likely to take any injury from the damp. It
was evident I was surrounded by natives, who had stolen
all these things during the short time I had been in my tent,
certainly not exceeding half an hour. The night was very
windy, and I had heard nothing; besides, I was encamped
in the midst of a very dense brush of large wide-spreading
tea-trees and other bushes, any of which would afford a
screen for a considerable number of natives. In daylight it
was impossible to see many yards in distance, and nothing
could be discerned at night. . . . As soon as I
missed my horizon-glass, and entertained the suspicion
of natives being about, I hurried into the tent, and
lighting a large blue light, run with it rapidly through
the bushes around me. The effect of this was very beauti-
ful amidst the darkness and gloom of the woods, and for a
great distance in every direction objects could be seen as
well as by day: the natives, however, were gone; and I
could only console myself by firing a couple of balls after
them through the underwood, to warn them of the danger
of intruding upon me again. I then put everything which
had been left outside into the tent, and kept watch for an
hour or two; but my visitors came no more. . . . Rising
very early, I set to work with an axe to clear away the
bushes from around my tent. I now discovered that the
natives had been concealed behind a large tea-tree not
twenty yards from the tent: there were numerous foot-
marks there, and the remains of fire-sticks which they had
brought with them, for a native rarely moves at night with-
out fire."
Mr Eyre seems to have no hope, in spite of
Capt. Sturt's cheering dispatches, that any inland
sea will ever be ultimately discovered behind this
vast unpromising table land. Can it be, he asks,
that the whole is one immense interminable desert,
"or an alternation of deserts and shallow lakes?"
Incidental to the narrative of the expeditions
are many illustrations of native character: but Mr
Eyre, as we before said, has collected all his many
years' experiences on this head into a separate
treatise or dissertation at the close of his work. The reader interested in the subject will find his
information curious and ample. The matters
treated of embrace not only the physical and moral
state of the aborigines; their habits of life, rude
government, and social relations; their language
and dialects; but also very interesting notices of
the effects of their contact with Europeans, and
some valuable suggestions for an improvement in
the system generally adopted towards them.
Our extracts are limited by our space: but to
even readers familiar with Captain Grey's excellent
dissertations, much of Mr Eyre's information will
be new and original.
HUSBAND AND WIFE.
"Wives are considered the absolute property of the husband, and can be given away, or exchanged, or lent, according to his caprice. A husband is denominated in the
Adelaide dialect, Yongarra, Martanya (the owner or pro-
prietor of a wife). Female children are betrothed usually
from early infancy, and such arrangements are usually ad-
hered to; still in many cases circumstances occur frequently
to cause an alteration; but if not, the girls generally go to
live with their husbands about the age of twelve, and some-
times even before that. Relatives nearer than cousins are
not allowed to marry, and this alliance does not generally
take place. Female orphans belong to the nearest male re-
lative, as also does a widow, instead of to the nearest male
relative of the husband, as was found to be the case in
Western Australia by Captain Grey. Two or three months
generally elapse before the widow goes to another hus-
band; but if the wife dies, the man takes another as soon
as he can get one. If a woman, having young children,
join another tribe, the children go with her; but I am not
aware whether they would remain permanently attached to
that tribe or not. Brothers often barter their sisters for
wives for themselves, but it can only be done with the
parents' consent, or after their death. If a wife be stolen,
war is always continued until she is given up, or another
female in her place.
"There is no ceremony connected with the undertaking
of marriage. In those cases where I have witnessed the
giving away of a wife, the woman was simply ordered by
the nearest male relative in whose disposal she was, to take
up her 'rocko,' the bag in which a female carries the effects
of her husband, and go to the man's camp to whom she had
been given. Marriage is not looked upon as any pledge of
chastity, indeed no such virtue is recognised. But little
real affection consequently exists between husbands and
wives, and young men value a wife principally for her ser-
vices as a slave; in fact, when asked why they are anxious
to obtain wives, their usual reply is, that they may get
wood, water, and food for them, and carry whatever pro-
perty they possess."
NATIVE MODESTY.
"Innate propriety of behaviour is also frequently exhi-
bited by the Aborigines in their natural state, in the modest
unassuming manner in which they take their positions to
observe what is going on, and in a total absence of any-
thing that is rude or offensive. It is true that the reverse
of this is also often to be met with; but I think it will
usually be found that it is among natives who have before
been in contact with Europeans, or where familiarities have
been used with them first, or an injudicious system of treat-
ment has been adopted towards them.
"Delicacy of feeling is not often laid to the charge of the
Aborigines, and yet I was witness to a singular instance of
it at King George's Sound. I was looking one evening at
the natives dancing, and who were, as they always are on
these occasions, in a state of complete nudity. In the
midst of the performance, one of the natives standing by as
a spectator, mentioned that a white woman was passing up
the road; and although this was some little distance away,
and the night was tolerably dark, they all with one accord
crossed over to the bushes where their cloaks were, put
them on, and resumed their amusement."
Some representations of native ornaments, wea-
pons, and implements and works of industry, in
this part of the book, are useful to the text.
THE THEATRICAL EXAMINER.
HAYMARKET.
The False Mr Pope is a retired Hammersmith
tradesman of about five feet four, with a Ramilie
wig and tail more than half as big as himself,
square-cut buckram skirts, long flapped white
waistcoat, and minute three-cornered hat, who is
passed off by a wag of a player upon a party of
petticoat admirers of Pope, for the celebrated au-
thor of the Dunciad. To fancy Mr Buckstone in
this predicament, is to have a very clear notion of
Mr Peake's amusing farce.
It is nicely presented; with abundance of pe-
ruke for the gentlemen, and of hoods, clustering
curls, cardinals, and little china, for the ladies; and
it perpetrates a vast many abominable jokes, which
nobody but the actors and actresses can possibly
be expected to laugh at. But this is the "moral."
The ladies are in such a state of frantic foregone
admiration of Mr Pope, that the more audacious
the flights of Mr Buckstone the wittier they are
taken to be; and though this is rather a danger-
ous experiment for a farce, the audience help it
ont with their good-nature.
Indeed it would take a troublesome amount of
the other quality to withstand Mr Buckstone's
practical points of drollery. When he takes off
his wig in a sudden heat, for example, and exposes
his small bald head, Swift's mouse under a canopy
of state is nothing to it. When he effects a series
of practical Rapes of the Lock, too, he uses the
scissors like a true poet. And when he passes
from doing to suffering, tastes the griefs as well as
glories of fame, and is well thrashed by Mr Culli's
chairman as he leaves the player's house,—the act
closed with a roar. There should have been no
second. There is nothing but stale repetition in
the second act. The ladies retort with a practical
joke of their own, which is much more remarkable
for its dullness than for any more lady-like quality.
LYCEUM.
An excellent new farce was played here on Monday night; better than any piece of its class which
we have seen for many a day. It has nicety of
character, and a good broad humour. You laugh,
and have no need to be ashamed of your mirth.
There is neither caricature nor coarseness. We
cannot stay to tell the plot (which is a plot, and
not told without some pains), but must briefly
counsel the playgoer to see Peter Jenkins. Mr
and Mrs Keeley, Mr Wigan and Mr Meadows,
complete an admirable cast. Mr Keeley is not
only an honest truth-telling fellow forced to tell
lies for a friend; but a confirmed little bachelor,
caught, willy-nilly, in the snares of matrimony.
His dilemmas are intense, and he does justice to
them.
FOREIGN NEWS.
FRANCE.
DEATH OF M. ROYER COLLARD.—This illustrious
citizen died on the 4th inst., at his estate at Chateauvieux,
near Saint-Aignan, in the 82nd year of his age. M.
Royer Collard had been President of the Chamber of De-
puties, Member of the French Academy, and Professor of
Philosophy at the College of France.
THE SLAVE TRADE CONVENTION.—"The vessels in-
tended to act against the slave trade are not," says the
'Constitutionnel,' "yet ready to proceed to the coasts of
Africa. They are not to set out for six weeks or two
months. Meanwhile communications are exchanged with
England every day on the subject of the mission which
the two navies are to fulfil together. Recently the Ad-
miralty has drawn up regulations for day and night sig-
nals, which the English and French cruisers are to make
use of, in order to mutually recognise each other. It ap-
pears that we have approved of all the dispositions of
these regulations. It is divided into two parts; the first
concerning sailing vessels, and the other steamers. The
English navy has been long occupied for its own use with
a regulation of this kind for steamers, collisions of which
are both frequent and dangerous. In France, nothing
has been done in that respect."
RUMOURED RETIREMENT OF MARSHAL SOULT.—A
letter from Castres announces that the Marquis de Mor-
nay has just arrived at Soultberg. If report can be be-
lieved, the marquis, who was at Beauvais for the Council-
General, quitted that town precipitately, in consequence
of a pressing invitation from the Minister of War. The
old marshal, who declares himself exceedingly fatigued
with the struggles and difficulties which he has to en-
counter, particularly from Algeria, and who is besides
tormented with a chronic cough, again talks of withdraw-
ing from office; but, as to withdraw at his age is to give
up public affairs for ever, he says, to
take such a determination without consulting his family.
The 'France' discredits the report of the Marshal's
retirement.
VISIT OF THE FRENCH PRINCES TO THE QUEEN OF
SPAIN.—On the 3rd inst., the Duke and Duchess de Ne-
mours and the Duke d'Aumale, after visiting Biarritz
and St Jean de Luz, arrived at the bridge which unites
France with Spain. There the Princes alighted from
their carriages and crossed the bridge on foot, accompa-
nied by Count Bresson, the French Ambassador, the Pre-
fect of the Department of the Lower Pyrenees; M. Aze-
vedo; Gen. Boyer, Aid-de-Camp of the Duke de Ne-
mours; Col. Jamin, Aid-de-Camp of the Duke d'Aumale,
&c. On reaching the Spanish territory they were com-
plimented by the Duke de San Carlos, a nobleman of the
Queen's Bedchamber, and Senor Arana, Master of the
Ceremonies of the Palace, in the name of the Queen, and
by Senors Olozabal and Aldamar, in that of the province
of Guipuzcoa. Gen. Barrenechea, commander of the pro-
vince, received the French Princes at the head of the
troops with all the honours due to their rank. The people,
on their side, loudly cheered them. The august party
slept at Tolosa, and entered Pampeluna on the following
day. Accounts from Bayonne of the 8th state that they
had returned to that town in good health, highly satisfied
with the reception given them, not only at Pampeluna,
but along the whole of their journey in Spain. The Duke
d'Aumale travelled back through the valley of Bastan on
horseback.
FUTURE RESIDENCE OF DON CARLOS.—The 'Constitu-
tionnel' says:—"The Marquis de Villafranca is hourly
expected at Paris. He comes to solicit, it is said, authori-
sation for Don Carlos and the Princess to proceed to
Rome, the climate of Bourges being injurious to the health
of the Princess, who was born in Brazil. If M. de
Villafranca does not obtain passports for Italy, he is
directed to demand from the French Government per-
mission for Don Carlos and the Princess to fix their resi-
dence in such town of the south as they may choose."
THE POPE'S SENTIMENTS TOWARDS FRANCE.—The
'Journal des Debats' states that on the occasion of the
celebration of the fêtes of St Louis in the French church at
Rome, the Pope and a considerable number of cardinals
attended. M. Rossi, the French Plenipotentiary, opened
the door of the carriage at the church door, and thanked
his Holiness for the honour he had designed to confer on the
French church. The Pope, in a voice so loud that he could
be heard by the crowd assembled around him, replied that
he had great pleasure in performing the pious duty, and
that he should be happy that that expression of his senti-
ments were known to the King of the French. After
prayers, his Holiness retired to an adjoining apartment,
where the ceremony of kissing his toe was gone through
by all the natives of France that presented themselves.

Strutt informs us that the Roman women, married as well as unmarried, used girdles, and besides them they sometimes wore a broad swath or bandage round their breasts, called strophium, which seems to have answered the purpose of the bodice or stays, and had a buckle or bandage on the left shoulder, and that the mitra or girdle of the Greeks probably resembled the strophium of the Romans. The annexed illustration represents a lady of Ancient Greece. He also speaks of the Muses as being described by Hesiod as being girt with golden "mitres," and goes on to inform us that Theocritus in one of his pastorals introduces a damsel complaining to a shepherd of his rudeness, saying he had loosened her mitra or girdle, and tells her he means to dedicate the same to Venus. So it will be seen that the waist and its adornment were considered at that early period of the world's history matters of no ordinary importance, and whether the term strophium, zone, mitra, custula, stays, bodice, or corset is made use of, the end sought to be obtained by their aid was the same.

Constant mention is made by early writers of the peplus as being a very elegant garment, and there are notices of it as far back as the Trojan war, and the ladies of Troy appear to have generally worn it. On the authority of Strutt, it may be stated to have been "a thin light mantle worn by Grecian ladies above the tunic;" and we read that Antinous presented to Penelope a beautiful large and variegated peplus, having twelve buckles of gold, with tongues neatly curved.
